newsitem.title: UK: Oil price stable, ignores mounting supply pressure.
newsitem.headline: Oil price stable, ignores mounting supply pressure.

text.p: World oil prices held their strength at the end of a bullish week where positive sentiment conquered negative supply and demand fundamentals.
The July futures conract for benchmark Brent blend crude oil traded at $19.50 a barrel at 1500gmt on Friday, up just a cent in very thin trade.
In New York NYMEX crude oil futures stood at $21.24 a barrel, down six cents in early business.
Crude oil rallied last week on the back of technical factors, institutional fund buying of futures and collective wish-fulfillment.
The bull run peaked at a two-month high on Monday at $19.72, nearly $2 up, with most analysts at a loss to explain its strength.
A stream of news this week has underlined that throughout this summer more oil will be pumped from the world's reservoirs than can be consumed.
But the bearish news has had litte effect on crude prices, which have remained steady.
The rise was kicked off last week by industry rumours that maintenance programmes would cut deeply into supplies of North Sea crude in June.
The fears proved exaggerated, even though in June some 12.5 million barrels less oil will be marketed from the North Sea than in May. Dealers said they had been expecting a bigger impact.
With doubt over loading programmes no longer supporting higher prices, oil traders have begun to question how long crude's rally can last.

Refined oil products have not enjoyed the same rise in price as the crude from which they are distilled. As a consequence refinery operators have seen their profit margins massacred, and this is expected to pressure values.
"Everyone expects crude to come off, but will it be a week, or two or three, that's what nobody knows," said one product trader, complaining crude's strength has slowed his business almost to a halt.
"We have to see further positive action in the products or the current crude rally will fail," said Leslie Nicholas, energy analyst at GNI Research. "The implications of that are obvious."
Crude dropped sharply earlier this year from $25 to around $18 as poor winter demand failed to soak up a flood of extra material.

Analysts began to talk in the early spring of crude values returning to the $13 to $18 range prevalent before last summer. The recent rally has thrown those predictions off course, but some say they may eventually be borne out.
